lesson.title: Depressants: Turning the Brake Pedal Down
lesson.summary: Depressants slow central nervous system activity, mainly by strengthening GABA, the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter system.
lesson.body:
Depressants are psychoactive drugs that slow down activity in the central nervous system, the functional opposite of stimulants. Rather than exciting neurons into firing more, depressants generally work by strengthening the brain's main inhibitory system, producing relaxation, sedation, slowed reaction time, and at high enough doses, dangerously suppressed breathing.

The neurotransmitter GABA is central to this story. GABA is the brain's primary inhibitory chemical, meaning that when it binds its receptor, called GABA A, it opens a channel that lets negatively charged chloride ions flow into the neuron, making that neuron less likely to fire. Most depressants work by making this braking system more effective rather than by silencing neurons directly.

Benzodiazepines, a class of prescription anti anxiety and sleep medications, bind to a site on the GABA A receptor that is distinct from where GABA itself attaches. Rather than opening the channel on their own, they make the channel open more easily and more often whenever GABA is present, essentially turning up the volume on the brain's existing braking signal. Barbiturates, an older and riskier class of sedatives, act on a nearby site with a more dangerous property: at sufficiently high doses they can help open the chloride channel even without GABA present, which is part of why barbiturate overdose is far more likely to be fatal than benzodiazepine overdose.

Alcohol is the most widely used depressant and works through a combination of mechanisms, which helps explain why its effects feel so broad. Like benzodiazepines, alcohol enhances GABA A receptor activity, contributing to relaxation and slowed reflexes. At the same time, it suppresses a separate class of receptors for glutamate, the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, removing some of the nervous system's accelerator at the same moment its brake is being pressed harder. That double action, more inhibition plus less excitation, is a major reason alcohol impairs judgment, coordination, and memory formation all at once.

Because alcohol and benzodiazepines act on overlapping sites on the same GABA A receptor, someone who has built tolerance to one often shows some cross tolerance to the other, and combining the two is especially dangerous. Each drug pushes the same inhibitory system further than either would alone, which is why mixing alcohol with benzodiazepines or barbiturates is a leading cause of accidental overdose deaths involving depressants.

Because depressants work by amplifying an existing inhibitory system rather than creating a new one, the brain can adapt to their constant presence by dialing down its own GABA sensitivity over time, a process explored in the chapter on drug tolerance. That same adaptation is exactly what makes suddenly stopping a depressant after heavy, long term use so physically dangerous.
